html:
The Sirionó are an Indigenous people of the forests and savannas of northeast Bolivia, in Beni and Santa Cruz departments. They speak a Tupi-Guarani language.

They were long a mobile people who hunted with very long bows, gathered, and farmed small plots, and they were pushed around by stronger neighbours and later by cattle ranchers. In the 1940s the American anthropologist Allan Holmberg lived among them and wrote Nomads of the Long Bow (1950), which made them famous in anthropology as a people struggling with hunger. Later scholars argued that their simple way of life was the result of epidemics and pressure from outsiders, not an ancient state. Their neighbours include the Guarayo and the Baure.
sum: The Sirionó are an Indigenous people of the forests and savannas of northeast Bolivia, in Beni and Santa Cruz departments. They speak a Tupi-Guarani language.
